lead: Both readings speak of trouble that does not have the last word. Paul tells the Corinthians how he was crushed in Asia until he despaired of life, and learned to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. In John, on the night before his Passion, Jesus warns his disciples that they will be scattered and will face persecution, and then gives them his peace: “take courage; I have conquered the world!” An apostle is not someone spared from trouble, but someone who has found that Christ is stronger.

set: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5), after a painful time in his relations with the Corinthians. He opens it by blessing “the God of all consolation” (1:3), who consoles us in every affliction so that we can console others. Now he tells them what he has just been through.

Asia here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Türkiye, with its capital at Ephesus, where Paul worked for a long time. He does not say what happened. Some connect it with the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41) or with the “wild animals” he fought there (1 Corinthians 15:32); others think of a grave illness. We do not know. What Paul wants them to know is not the details but what God did.
str: v. 8: the affliction in Asia: crushed beyond strength, despairing of life.
v. 9: the sentence of death, so that we would rely on God who raises the dead.
v. 10: he rescued us, he will rescue us, on him we have set our hope.
v. 11: the Corinthians’ prayers help, so that many will give thanks.
kw: Literally pressure, crushing, as grapes are pressed. It is the same word Jesus uses in today’s Gospel: “In the world you face persecution” (John 16:33). The apostle’s life is lived under this pressure, and God’s consolation meets him there.
The word apokrima means an official answer or verdict. Paul felt as if the verdict of death had already been given. That verdict became a lesson in trust.
vv: we were so utterly, unbearably crushed that we despaired of life itself.
Paul does not pretend to be stronger than he was. He speaks openly of despair. Holiness is not the absence of fear but faith that holds on through it.
so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
A prayer of Israel, still said daily, praises God “who gives life to the dead”. Paul has learned it in his own body: the God who raised Jesus is the one to lean on when every human hope fails.
as you also join in helping us by your prayers, so that many will give thanks on our behalf
The great apostle asks for the prayers of a troubled community. Prayer joins Christians together, and the answer to many prayers becomes the thanksgiving of many.
ch: The Church sees in this passage the meaning of Christian suffering: it can teach us to rely on God and unite us to Christ’s death and Resurrection. The Catechism teaches that intercession, asking on behalf of another, is a prayer that conforms us to the prayer of Jesus, and that the first Christian communities lived this fellowship intensely, as Paul gave them a share in his ministry through their prayers (CCC 2634–2636).

set: These are the last words of Jesus’ long farewell discourse at the Last Supper (John 13–16), just before his great prayer to the Father (chapter 17). He has spoken of going away, of the coming of the Spirit, and of sorrow turned into joy like a mother’s after childbirth (16:21). Now he sums up: he came from the Father and is going back to the Father.
The disciples think they understand at last. Jesus gently shows them that their faith will soon be tested: within hours they will run away. Yet he speaks these words so that they may have peace.
str: vv. 25–28: no longer in figures: the Father himself loves you; I came from the Father and go to the Father.
vv. 29–30: the disciples: now you speak plainly; we believe you came from God.
vv. 31–32: “Do you now believe?” You will be scattered; yet I am not alone.
v. 33: peace in me; persecution in the world; take courage, I have conquered the world.
kw: A saying with a hidden meaning, a riddle or image, like the good shepherd (10:6) or the woman in labour (16:21). The “hour” when Jesus speaks plainly is the hour of his death and Resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit who leads into all truth (16:13).
Speech that is frank and without fear. After Pentecost the apostles speak about Jesus with the same parrēsia, boldness (Acts 4:13, 29, 31).

The perfect tense: a victory already won whose effect remains. Jesus says it before the cross, as if the battle were over. The same verb appears again in 1 John 5:4: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.”
vv: for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.
Jesus does not need to persuade an unwilling Father. The Father’s love comes first and meets the disciples who love his Son.
you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.
Mark recalls the prophecy “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). Jesus knows they will fail, and he still loves them and promises peace.
In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!
Jesus does not promise a life without trouble. He promises himself: peace “in me”, and a victory that is already his.
ch: The Catechism teaches that from the time of his Passover Jesus teaches us to pray to the Father “in his name”, and that faith in the Son introduces the disciples into the knowledge of the Father (CCC 2614). The Church has always read “I have conquered the world” as the source of the martyrs’ courage. Pope St John Paul II began his ministry in 1978 with the words “Do not be afraid! Open wide the doors for Christ”, a call that comes from the same confidence in the Risen Lord.

qa: Jesus says, “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf.” Does Jesus not intercede for us?

He does. Scripture says that Christ always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). In this verse Jesus means that the Father does not need to be won over: “the Father himself loves you.” When we pray in Jesus’ name, we are not standing outside, asking him to persuade God; we pray united with the Son, as children loved by the Father.
study: Paul learned to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. When did a difficult time teach me to trust God more?
Jesus says, “In the world you face persecution. But take courage.” Whom do I know who needs to hear this today, and how can I bring them Christ’s peace?
